problem: The convergence condition is corrupted: "At R, this tends to 0 when 1−p1, giving value 1/(p−1)." The inequality is missing, so the sentence states no condition and a student cannot tell why the limit is 0. The value 1/(p−1) then appears from nowhere.
fix: At R, x^(1−p)/(1−p) tends to 0 when 1−p < 0, that is when p > 1, giving the value 0 − 1/(1−p) = 1/(p−1). When p < 1, 1−p > 0 and the expression grows without bound, so the integral diverges.

problem: The condition is corrupted and contradicts the table: "∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx converges exactly when p 1 the term c^(1−p) grows." As written, the sentence both drops the inequality and reads as if p > 1 gives convergence, while the table correctly says p < 1 converges.
fix: ∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx converges exactly when p < 1. The proper integral from c to 1 equals 1/(1−p) − c^(1−p)/(1−p). For p < 1, c^(1−p) → 0 as c→0⁺, so the limit is 1/(1−p). For p > 1, 1−p < 0 and c^(1−p) grows without bound. For p = 1, the value ln(1/c) grows. Hence p = 1 diverges.
